key_findings.finding: The most likely diagnosis is disseminated Taenia solium cysticercosis—specifically neurocysticercosis with ocular/subretinal cysticercosis. The combination of new-onset seizure, multiple small parenchymal ring-enhancing lesions, directly visualized subretinal cysts, CSF eosinophilia, and origin from an endemic region is characteristic; PubTator identifies neurocysticercosis and submacular cysticercosis as distinct recognized entities, and a neurocysticercosis series lists direct visualization of subretinal parasites as a diagnostic criterion.

source_tools.relevance: Disease/entity normalization for neurocysticercosis and submacular cysticercosis
Clinical evidence linking neurocysticercosis to subretinal parasites

key_findings.finding: The transmission route is ingestion of T. solium eggs shed in human feces—typically via fecally contaminated food or water or hand-to-mouth transmission from a human tapeworm carrier. Cysticercosis is therefore not acquired by eating undercooked pork; pork containing larval cysticerci causes intestinal taeniasis, whereas ingestion of eggs causes tissue-invasive larval cysts in brain and eye.

source_tools.relevance: Disease definition explicitly states cysticercosis results from T. solium larvae ingested via feces of a human with a tapeworm

key_findings.finding: Toxoplasmosis is a less likely choice despite ring-enhancing lesions: cerebral toxoplasmosis is classically associated with HIV/AIDS or another immunosuppressed state, and HIV-negative cases are described as extremely rare. The subretinal cysts and CSF eosinophilia instead support helminthic cysticercosis rather than Toxoplasma encephalitis.

source_tools.relevance: Disease ontology description says cerebral toxoplasmosis primarily arises with immunologic deficiency syndromes
PubMed case report characterizes HIV-seronegative cerebral toxoplasmosis as extremely rare and reports ring-enhancing lesions without the ocular-cyst finding
